items.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998
items.q: And at the end he came out and we were talking and kicking stones and talking, and he said, “you know, you play like I think.”

ctx.x: And you know usually when we do a standard or something that people know, we try to honor it the way the composer wrote it, I mean pretty much so. You know you try to sing the melody the way — the right notes he wanted and the right chords. But then if it’s a song that’s really been used a lot and done by a lot of people, then we feel we can take more liberty. They’ve heard it that way. They’ve heard it that way a thousand times, and now we can start out and maybe do it a little differently, maybe change a note…

And my greatest compliment in the last couple of years came from Johnny Mandel. He came in to hear us at the Jazz Bakery in Los Angeles. We had a very good rhythm section that came with us from San Francisco. It was popping, everything was great. And we did one of his songs called “The Shining Sea,” which is a gorgeous melody. And I found — I explored ways to bring out more impressionistic sounds in it, just all kind of painting. And at the end he came out and we were talking and kicking stones and talking, and…

The other one that I could relate is that Alec Wilder once said that we often break the rules but you don’t mind it. And he’s a stickler. He doesn’t like it when you take too many liberties, but he says, “well Roy changes my chords but usually they’re for the better.”
